sections.title: Basic Concept of Syllogism
sections.content: In Syllogism, 2 or 3 statements are given followed by 2 conclusions. You have to decide whether the conclusions logically follow from the statements. The answer must be definitely true based on the given statements, not based on general knowledge.

sections.title: Important Keywords
sections.content: All means the entire group is included in another group. Some means at least one part is common. No means there is no common part between two groups. Some not means at least one part is excluded.

sections.title: Basic Mental Venn Diagram
sections.content: For All A are B, draw circle A completely inside circle B. For Some A are B, show overlapping area between A and B. For No A are B, draw two separate circles. For Some A are not B, show part of A outside B.

sections.title: Two-Statement Example
sections.content: Statements: All cats are animals. Some animals are black. Conclusion: Some cats are black. This does not definitely follow because we do not know whether the black animals include cats.

sections.title: Three-Statement Example
sections.content: Statements: All A are B. All B are C. Conclusion: All A are C. This definitely follows because A is fully inside B and B is fully inside C.

sections.title: Basic Either Or Case
sections.content: Either Or occurs when two conclusions are opposite in nature and only one can be true. If one must definitely be true but not both together, then Either I or II follows.

sections.title: 2–3 Step Solution Method
sections.content: Step 1: Identify keywords like All, Some, No. Step 2: Form a mental Venn diagram. Step 3: Check whether the conclusion is true in every possible case.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Treating Some as All. 2. Assuming possibility as certainty. 3. Ignoring negative statements. 4. Not checking both conclusions separately.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Syllogism is based on logic and Venn diagram imagination. A conclusion follows only if it is true in all possible cases based on the statements.

tricks.title: All + All Rule
tricks.explanation: If All A are B and All B are C, then All A are C.
tricks.example: All students are learners. All learners are humans. Therefore, all students are humans.

tricks.title: All to Some Rule
tricks.explanation: If All A are B, then Some A are B is always true.
tricks.example: All dogs are animals, so some dogs are animals.

tricks.title: No Relationship Rule
tricks.explanation: If No A are B, then Some A are not B is definitely true.
tricks.example: No cats are dogs, so some cats are not dogs.

tricks.title: Some Means Minimum One
tricks.explanation: Some means at least one, not all.
tricks.example: Some players are singers means only a few, not every player.

tricks.title: Some + Some Trap
tricks.explanation: Some A are B and Some B are C does not guarantee relation between A and C.
tricks.example: Some students are athletes. Some athletes are singers. We cannot say some students are singers.

tricks.title: Negative Statement Impact
tricks.explanation: If a statement contains No, the conclusion often becomes negative.
tricks.example: No birds are mammals, so some mammals are not birds.

tricks.title: Middle Term Check
tricks.explanation: In three statements, the middle term connects two groups. Use it to find relation between first and last term.
tricks.example: All A are B and All B are C, so check A and C.

tricks.title: Either Or Basic Check
tricks.explanation: Either Or works only when two conclusions are opposite and only one can be true.
tricks.example: Some A are B or Some A are not B.

tricks.title: Check Both Conclusions Separately
tricks.explanation: First verify Conclusion I, then Conclusion II, then check Either Or.
tricks.example: Do not combine them without checking individually.

tricks.title: Certainty Rule
tricks.explanation: Conclusion must be definitely true in every possible diagram.
tricks.example: If one possible diagram makes it false, it does not follow.
